Southwest Airlines 1380 · Boeing 737-7H4

Blade No. 13

A Boeing 737 out of New York climbs through 32,648 feet. Then a fan blade breaks inside the left engine. One person died.

A loud bang, then shaking

A window torn out

At the bang, a piece of debris strikes the fuselage beside a window, and the window is gone. The cabin loses its pressure fast and a warning horn sounds. It is the first known loss of a whole passenger window on a Boeing 737.

The checklist

Nearest in time

The checklist tells the crew to plan to land at the nearest suitable airport. The airline's handbook counts nearest in flying time. From 32,000 feet, the NTSB found, Harrisburg or Philadelphia would take about the same time.

Landing11:20

Down in Philadelphia

Unsure how the jet will handle, the captain lands at about 171 knots with the wing flaps at only 5 degrees. One passenger is fatally injured, and eight others have minor injuries.

The loose blade struck the engine case.

Where did the blade hit the case?

{{ o.t }}
{{ verdict }}

Certification tests released a blade at twelve o'clock. A hit at the bottom sent loads into the engine cover its design never counted on.

Dents and marks beside the missing window at row 14 fit the size and shape of one recovered part.

Which part made those marks?

{{ o.t }}
{{ verdict }}

The aft latch keeper, a latch part at the back of the engine cover, flew over the engine and wing and struck beside seat 14A.

pages.tpl:
7 of 8
Cause

The probable cause

A hidden fatigue crack broke a fan blade. The blow tore the engine cover apart, and one piece knocked out the window at row 14.
Also found
  • The pilots' qualifications and health and the airline's maintenance were not factors.
  • The NTSB says what followed the blade failure could not have been predicted from the certification tests.
The official wording
Words on this page
fatigue crack a crack that grows a tiny step each time a part is loaded and unloaded, until the part breaks
Next

In the report's words

“The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was a low-cycle fatigue crack in the dovetail of fan blade No. 13, which resulted in the fan blade separating in flight and impacting the engine fan case at a location that was critical to the structural integrity and performance of the fan cowl structure. This impact led to the in-flight separation of fan cowl components, including the inboard fan cowl aft latch keeper, which struck the fuselage near a cabin window and caused the window to depart from the airplane, the cabin to rapidly depressurize, and the passenger fatality.”

NTSB report AAR-19/03, word for word

Lessons

What it teaches

  1. 1A crack can slip through the checks of its day, so the checks themselves had to change.
  2. 2Where a broken blade hits can decide what else breaks.
  3. 3Crew belong strapped in for landing in case an evacuation is needed. The NTSB says it was not a factor here.

pages.tpl:
8 of 8
Lessons

What changed

  1. 1The FAA now requires repeated ultrasonic checks of every fan blade on these engines.
  2. 2By August 2019 the newer checks had found 15 cracked blades on separate engines.
  3. 3The NTSB asked for a redesigned engine cover on all 737 NG jets.
Words on this page
ultrasonic inspection a check that sends high frequency sound into a part to find cracks hidden below the surface
737 NG the Boeing 737 Next Generation family, the 737-600, -700, -800 and -900 models built from the late 1990s
